performers: John Harrison, violin; Wichita State University Chamber Players; Robert Turizziani, conductor
question: Can you follow the singing line and the rain-like accompaniment at the same time?
intro: A sustained violin melody suggests warmth indoors while plucked orchestral violins evoke rain outside. The first phrase reaches B♭ major; its varied continuation finds the way back to E♭.

sections.label: Varied continuation · approximate
sections.mNote: the melody begins again in B♭ and returns towards E♭

cues.title: Singing above the rain
cues.text: The solo violin bows a connected melody while the orchestral violins pluck their notes. Low strings keep a quieter pulse beneath the two. The score distinguishes the rain outside from the sustained line associated with comfort indoors.
cues.evidence: Mutopia II labels the orchestral violin part La Pioggia and Pizziccati forte, the solo part Largo–Solo, and the bass Sempre Piano: https://www.mutopiaproject.org/cgibin/piece-info.cgi?id=351.

cues.title: One line, many small attacks
cues.text: Listen beneath the soloist’s long phrase for the accompaniment’s separate plucked attacks. The two layers keep different kinds of continuity: the melody connects pitches, while the accompaniment keeps restarting its sound.
cues.evidence: This is a texture-wide prompt based on the written pizzicato parts, not a timed claim about a new entrance: https://www.mutopiaproject.org/cgibin/piece-info.cgi?id=351.
cues.how: A general description of this stretch of music.

cues.title: A sheltered winter scene
cues.text: The sonnet places the listener beside a fire while rain falls outside. Unlike the first movement’s shivering, this movement holds two contrasting environments together rather than moving rapidly from one bodily action to another.
cues.evidence: Winter’s second-movement stanza contrasts the fire indoors with rain outside: https://nac-cna.ca/en/event/notes/36996.

cues.title: The melody finds a route home
cues.text: The continuation begins from the first phrase’s B♭-major destination, then brings the music back towards E♭. It is a varied restatement, not a second performance of the same eight bars.
cues.evidence: The movement analysis identifies an eight-bar opening ending in B♭, followed by a varied restatement that returns to E♭. Mutopia bars 9–16 show the changed continuation; the report places an important change at 1:14, inside that tonal return: https://www.teoria.com/en/articles/2022/vivaldi-seasons/inverno/02.php; https://www.mutopiaproject.org/cgibin/piece-info.cgi?id=351.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: A live performance in Kansas
cues.text: This performance comes from a Wichita State University concert on 6 February 2000, with John Harrison as soloist and Robert Turizziani conducting. Its modern concert setting is distinct from the eighteenth-century pastoral scene in the score.
cues.evidence: The Commons recording description identifies the date, venue and performers: https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:11_-_Vivaldi_Winter_mvt_2_Largo_-_John_Harrison_violin.ogg.

transitions.title: The dominant becomes a new starting point
transitions.how: The opening eight-bar span closes in B♭ major, the dominant of E♭. The solo melody begins a related shape from that new position and alters its continuation to return home. The plucked accompaniment remains, so the change is heard through pitch and phrasing rather than a replacement of instruments.
transitions.evidence: The score’s first eight bars and bar-9 restatement establish the form. The boundary is a score-proportion estimate around 0:58, where the report shows the relatively low level of the phrase ending, not an exact note alignment: https://www.teoria.com/en/articles/2022/vivaldi-seasons/inverno/02.php; https://www.mutopiaproject.org/cgibin/piece-info.cgi?id=351.

transitions.title: The long final note outlasts the pattern
transitions.how: The returning phrase resolves to E♭. The soloist sustains that note while the plucked figures and quiet bass complete the final bars, then all parts settle on the closing harmony. The melody can stop moving before the accompaniment finishes.
transitions.evidence: Mutopia bars 16–18 tie the solo E♭ through the final bars and retain moving accompaniment before the fermata. The report’s change at 1:52 and declining activity after 2:00 support an approximate closing region: https://www.mutopiaproject.org/cgibin/piece-info.cgi?id=351.

composer.epithet: A violinist and theatre composer who made the returning orchestral refrain organise a soloist’s changing keys, textures and physical risks.
facts: Violin with his father Giovanni Battista, a violinist at St Mark’s, Venice
Violin teacher at the Ospedale della Pietà from 1703; maestro de’ concerti from 1716; theatre work in Venice and other cities
More than 500 concertos; operas, sacred vocal music, sonatas and chamber cantatas
composer.background:
Vivaldi was born in Venice, the son of a barber who became a professional violinist at St Mark’s. Giovanni Battista Vivaldi taught his son the violin and remained involved in his musical work. Antonio trained for the priesthood and was ordained in 1703, acquiring the nickname il prete rosso, the red priest, from his hair. He soon ceased regularly celebrating Mass, later explaining that a condition of tightness in the chest prevented him. He travelled extensively, taught and managed operatic productions.

In 1703 the Ospedale della Pietà appointed him violin teacher. The Pietà was a charitable institution that cared for abandoned children; its celebrated performing body consisted of girls and women whose training could continue into adult professional responsibility within the institution. Concerts and services attracted Venetian patrons and foreign visitors. Vivaldi’s employment was periodically renewed and sometimes interrupted, but the connection endured for decades. The players supplied a practical laboratory: a concerto could be written for a particular instrumental skill, tried in performance, and followed by another that changed the problem.
